Diffusion IRT for the LEVANTE mental rotation task

How to fit a Q-diffusion IRT model with diffIRT, and what its item and person parameters tell us

1. What the model is

Standard IRT uses only the accuracy of each response. A diffusion IRT model also uses the response time. Each response is the outcome of a noisy evidence-accumulation (Wiener) process between a correct and an incorrect boundary, which gives a joint likelihood for accuracy and response time. The Q-diffusion model of Molenaar, Tuerlinckx and van der Maas (2015) is meant for ability data. It splits the usual diffusion parameters into a person part and an item part:

quantity person item
boundary separation \(\gamma_p\) \(1/a_i\)
drift rate \(\theta_p\) \(1/v_i\)
non-decision time \(T_{er,i}\)

so that the person-by-item boundary separation is \(\gamma_p / a_i\) and the drift rate is \(\theta_p / v_i\). Because the process starts midway between the boundaries, the probability of a correct response is

\[P(x_{pi}=1) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(\frac{\gamma_p}{a_i}\cdot\frac{\theta_p}{v_i}\right).\]

Two things follow that matter for interpreting the parameters:

  • Larger \(v_i\) means a harder item (lower drift), so \(v_i\) plays the role of difficulty.
  • Accuracy has a floor of 0.5 (as the drift goes to zero, the process becomes a coin flip). That matches the guessing parameter fixed at 0.5 in the paper’s 2PL models for this two-alternative task.

The person parameters are log-normal, \(\log\gamma_p \sim N(0,\omega_\gamma^2)\) and \(\log\theta_p \sim N(0,\omega_\theta^2)\), so \(\theta_p\) is a person’s speed of information accumulation (the analogue of ability) and \(\gamma_p\) is their caution (speed-accuracy trade-off). Both are integrated out by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, with item parameters estimated by marginal maximum likelihood.

2. Data

data/mrot_rt_trial.rds has one row per trial (run, item, correct, reaction time in seconds). diffIRT needs a persons \(\times\) items matrix of responses and one of response times, with NA for unseen items.

  • Persons are assessments (runs) with at least one usable trial.
  • Items. The task is adaptive, so a run sees only a few of the 81 concrete stimuli (some twice). Columns are stimulus \(\times\) occurrence within the run, the same unit as in the paper’s all_items IRT models, so that repeated stimuli are separate items.
  • Item classes. Parameters are shared by the columns of a class (stimulus \(\times\) angle: 2D duck, 2D rabbit, 3D shape, 12 classes in all), exactly as the paper’s 2PL does. This gives 12 \(a_i\), 12 \(v_i\) and a few \(T_{er}\) values rather than 243 free item parameters.
  • Trimming. Responses faster than 0.5 s are dropped as anticipations (1.3% of trials), as are responses at the 30 s time limit. Section 3 explains why 0.5 s.
trials <- read_rds(here("data/mrot_rt_trial.rds"))
rt_min <- 0.5; rt_max <- 29.9

d <- trials |>
  filter(rt_s >= rt_min, rt_s < rt_max) |>
  arrange(run_id, trial_number) |>
  mutate(occ = row_number(), .by = c(run_id, item_original),
         col = paste(item_uid, item_original, occ, sep = "|"))

cols <- d |> distinct(col, item_uid, item_group) |> arrange(item_uid, col)
runs <- d |> distinct(run_id, user_id, site, dataset, adaptive, age) |> arrange(run_id)

to_mat <- \(v) d |> select(run_id, col, all_of(v)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = all_of(v)) |>
  arrange(run_id) |> select(-run_id) |> as.matrix() |> _[, cols$col]
rt <- to_mat("rt_s")
x  <- to_mat("correct"); storage.mode(x) <- "numeric"
stopifnot(identical(is.na(rt), is.na(x)))

cat(nrow(rt), "persons,", ncol(rt), "item columns,", n_distinct(cols$item_uid), "item classes;",
    sum(!is.na(rt)), "trials,", round(100 * (1 - nrow(d) / nrow(trials)), 1), "% dropped\n")
## 1158 persons, 81 item columns, 12 item classes; 49047 trials, 1.3 % dropped
class_obs <- d |>
  summarise(n = n(), accuracy = mean(correct), mean_rt = mean(rt_s), median_rt = median(rt_s),
            .by = item_uid) |>
  arrange(item_uid)
class_obs |> mutate(across(c(accuracy, mean_rt, median_rt), f3))

Accuracy falls and response time rises with the rotation angle, and the 3D shapes are much slower than the 2D animals.

3. Fitting the model

Constraints

diffIRT(rt, x, model, constrain, start, se, control) takes a constrain vector of length \(3 n_{items}+2\) giving, for each column, which parameter it uses: first the \(a\)’s, then the \(v\)’s, then the \(T_{er}\)’s, then the two scale parameters \(\omega_\gamma\) and \(\omega_\theta\). Columns with the same integer share a parameter, ids must run consecutively from 1, and 0 means fixed (at the value in start). Sharing parameters within an item class is therefore just a matter of building the vector:

cls <- cols$item_uid
nit <- ncol(rt)
k   <- as.integer(factor(cls))      # item class of each column (1..12)
nc  <- max(k)

# non-decision time shared within 2D and within 3D classes (see below)
kt  <- as.integer(factor(grepl("_3d_", cls)))
nt  <- max(kt)

constrain <- c(k,                       # a_i: one per class
               nc + k,                  # v_i: one per class
               2 * nc + kt,             # Ter: one per 2D/3D group
               2 * nc + nt + 1,         # omega_gamma
               2 * nc + nt + 2)         # omega_theta
length(constrain) == 3 * nit + 2
## [1] TRUE
max(constrain)                          # number of free parameters
## [1] 28

Starting value for Ter

By default diffIRT starts from EZ-diffusion estimates. For these data that start is poor: the optimiser ran into a local optimum with several non-decision times at exactly 0, and the fit was worse than a fit from a better start. Raising the fast-response cutoff does not cure this, since \(T_{er}\) simply follows the cutoff (about 0.7 s below it). A start of 0.3 s works. Passing a value in start for the \(T_{er}\) slots (and NA for everything else, which keeps the default) does that:

start <- c(rep(NA, 2 * nit), rep(0.3, nit), NA, NA)

The fit

The optimiser runs once for each number of quadrature points in nq, restarting from the previous solution, so c(7, 15) is a cheap coarse fit followed by a finer one. se = TRUE gives standard errors from the numerical Hessian.

fit_time <- system.time(
  fit <- diffIRT(rt, x, model = "Q", constrain = constrain, start = start, se = TRUE,
                 control = list(nq = c(7, 15), trace = 0))
)
## Fitting the Q-diffusion IRT model. Please wait . . .
c(elapsed_s = unname(fit_time["elapsed"]), converged = fit$conv == 0, minus2LL = fit$totLL,
  n_par = fit$npars, AIC = fit$AIC, BIC = fit$BIC)
##  elapsed_s  converged   minus2LL      n_par        AIC        BIC 
##     10.763      1.000 253385.323     28.000 253441.323 253582.847

This is the optimised build of diffIRT (branch fast-kernel). The same fit with the original package did not finish a 70-person subset in 20 minutes; see README.md.

Is 0.3 s sensible?

Fixing \(T_{er}\) at a grid of values (same data, same model) gives a profile with a minimum near 0.3 s, so the data support the start value rather than merely tolerating it:

prof <- tibble(ter = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)) |>
  mutate(file = here("models", sprintf("diffirt_q_rtmin0.5_fast_nall_nq7-15_terfixed%s.rds", ter)),
         minus2LL = map_dbl(file, \(f) if (file.exists(f)) read_rds(f)$fit$totLL else NA_real_)) |>
  select(-file)
prof <- bind_rows(prof, tibble(ter = NA, minus2LL = fit$totLL)) |>
  mutate(model = c(rep("Ter fixed", 4), "Ter free (2D/3D, started at 0.3 s)"), .before = 1)
prof

4. Item parameters

first <- match(1:nc, k)
items <- tibble(
  item_uid = levels(factor(cls)),
  a = fit$par[first],           a_se = fit$std.err[first],
  v = fit$par[nit + first],     v_se = fit$std.err[nit + first],
  ter = fit$par[2 * nit + first], ter_se = fit$std.err[2 * nit + first]) |>
  separate(item_uid, c(NA, "type", "stimulus", "angle"), sep = "_", remove = FALSE, convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(label = paste(type, stimulus, angle), type = toupper(type))
omega <- tibble(parameter = c("omega_gamma", "omega_theta"), estimate = tail(fit$par, 2), se = tail(fit$std.err, 2))
items |> select(item_uid, a, a_se, v, v_se, ter, ter_se) |> mutate(across(-item_uid, f3))
omega |> mutate(across(-parameter, f3))

Drift-based difficulty \(v\) rises with angle within every stimulus and is roughly four times larger for the 3D shape than the 2D animals. Boundary separation \(a\) is nearly constant across classes, and the non-decision time is shared within 2D/3D by construction. Standard errors are small. They come from a numerical Hessian at 15 quadrature points, so treat them as a lower bound.

ggplot(items, aes(angle, v, colour = stimulus, shape = type)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = v - 2 * v_se, ymax = v + 2 * v_se)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(items$angle)) +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (degrees)", y = expression(paste("Item difficulty ", v[i])), colour = NULL, shape = NULL)

5. Comparison with the paper’s 2PL item estimates

The paper fits a multigroup 2PL (guessing fixed at 0.5, scalar invariance across datasets) with the same twelve item classes. The coefficients are in models/mrot_coef.rds. In mirt’s parameterisation \(P = g + (1-g)\,\mathrm{logistic}(a_1\theta + d)\), with difficulty \(b=-d/a_1\).

irt <- read_rds(here("models/mrot_coef.rds")) |>
  filter(model_set == "multigroup_dataset", subset == "all_items", itemtype == "2pl", invariance == "scalar") |>
  distinct(item_uid = item, a1, d, b = difficulty, g)
cmp <- items |> left_join(irt, by = "item_uid") |>
  mutate(av = a * v,                       # product enters the Q-model logit as theta*gamma / (a*v)
         slope_q = 1 / (a * v))           # change in logit per unit of gamma*theta
stopifnot(!anyNA(cmp$b))
cmp |> select(item_uid, `2PL b` = b, `2PL a1` = a1, `Q: v` = v, `Q: a` = a, `Q: a*v` = av) |>
  mutate(across(-item_uid, f3))

Correlations across the 12 classes

In the Q model the logit is \((\gamma_p\theta_p)/(a_i v_i)\), so the product \(a_i v_i\) is the item’s overall hardness, and its reciprocal is the item’s slope relative to the person’s speed. Difficulty and discrimination are therefore tied together in a way they are not in the 2PL: a larger \(v_i\) lowers accuracy and also flattens the item’s response to \(\theta\).

cor_tab <- function(x, y, label) tibble(
  comparison = label,
  pearson  = cor(x, y), spearman = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
bind_rows(
  cor_tab(cmp$b,  log(cmp$v),         "2PL difficulty b vs log v"),
  cor_tab(cmp$b,  log(cmp$av),        "2PL difficulty b vs log(a*v)"),
  cor_tab(cmp$b,  cmp$ter,            "2PL difficulty b vs Ter"),
  cor_tab(cmp$a1, cmp$slope_q,        "2PL discrimination a1 vs Q slope 1/(a*v)"),
  cor_tab(cmp$a1, cmp$a,              "2PL discrimination a1 vs Q boundary a"),
  cor_tab(cmp$a1, log(cmp$v),         "2PL discrimination a1 vs log v")) |>
  mutate(across(-comparison, \(z) round(z, 2)))

The difficulty-like parameter lines up very closely with the 2PL difficulty: \(r = .96\) over the 12 classes. The 2D/3D gap drives part of that, so the within-2D values below matter, and they are still high. Non-decision time is also lower for the harder (3D) classes, but with only two estimated values (\(T_{er}\) is shared within 2D and within 3D) that correlation carries no information. Discrimination does not match: across all classes the 2PL \(a_1\) is weakly and negatively related to the Q slope \(1/(a_i v_i)\), and within the 2D classes the sign is clearly opposite, because 2PL slopes rise with angle while the Q-model slope falls as \(v_i\) rises.

two <- filter(cmp, type == "2D")
c(`within 2D (n = 9): b vs log v` = cor(two$b, log(two$v)),
  `within 2D: b vs log(a*v)`     = cor(two$b, log(two$av)),
  `within 2D: a1 vs 1/(a*v)`     = cor(two$a1, two$slope_q),
  `within 2D: a1 vs log v`       = cor(two$a1, log(two$v))) |> round(2)
## within 2D (n = 9): b vs log v      within 2D: b vs log(a*v) 
##                          0.89                          0.89 
##      within 2D: a1 vs 1/(a*v)        within 2D: a1 vs log v 
##                         -0.84                          0.87
p1 <- ggplot(cmp, aes(b, log(v), colour = stimulus, shape = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey50", linewidth = .4) +
  labs(x = "2PL difficulty b", y = "Q-diffusion log v", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
p2 <- ggplot(cmp, aes(a1, slope_q, colour = stimulus, shape = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "2PL discrimination a1", y = "Q-diffusion slope 1/(a*v)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, guides = "collect")

Predicted accuracy and response time

The parameters are not on the same scale, so compare what they predict. For each person with both scores, compute the probability of a correct response to each item class from (i) the 2PL with the paper’s \(\hat\theta\) and (ii) the Q-diffusion model with the person’s own \((\hat\gamma_p,\hat\theta_p)\) from factest(), and compare both with the observed accuracy. The scores are the same persons’ EAP estimates, so both models are evaluated in-sample.

sc <- factest(fit)                     # EAP gamma (col 1) and theta (col 2) for each person
persons <- bind_cols(runs, tibble(gamma = sc[, 1], theta = sc[, 2])) |>
  left_join(read_rds(here("models/mrot_scores.rds")) |> filter(model_set == "multigroup_dataset") |>
              select(run_id, theta_irt = metric_value), by = "run_id")
colSums(is.na(persons[c("gamma", "theta", "theta_irt")]))
##     gamma     theta theta_irt 
##         0         0         0
pred <- d |>
  select(run_id, item_uid, correct, rt_s) |>
  left_join(persons |> select(run_id, gamma, theta, theta_irt), by = "run_id") |>
  left_join(cmp |> select(item_uid, a, v, ter, a1, d, g), by = "item_uid") |>
  mutate(p_2pl = g + (1 - g) * plogis(a1 * theta_irt + d),
         A  = gamma / a,                        # person x item boundary separation
         nu = theta / v,                        # person x item drift rate
         p_q = plogis(A * nu),
         # mean RT of the Wiener process starting midway: Ter + A/(2 nu) * tanh(A nu / 2)
         rt_q = ter + ifelse(abs(nu) < 1e-8, A^2 / 4, A / (2 * nu) * tanh(A * nu / 2)))

by_class <- pred |>
  summarise(observed = mean(correct), `2PL` = mean(p_2pl, na.rm = TRUE), `Q-diffusion` = mean(p_q),
            .by = item_uid) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(item_uid, observed), names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted")
ggplot(by_class, aes(observed, predicted, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey70") + geom_point(size = 2) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(.5, 1), ylim = c(.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Observed accuracy of class", y = "Mean predicted accuracy", colour = NULL)

fit_stats <- pred |> filter(!is.na(p_2pl)) |>
  summarise(across(c(p_2pl, p_q), list(
    brier = \(p) mean((correct - p)^2),
    logloss = \(p) -mean(correct * log(p) + (1 - correct) * log(1 - p))), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"))
fit_stats |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("model", "stat"), names_pattern = "p_(.*)_(.*)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, `2pl` = "2PL", q = "Q-diffusion"), across(-model, \(z) round(z, 4)))

The 2PL predicts accuracy a little better (Brier 0.127 vs 0.133, log loss 0.386 vs 0.404). That is expected: it is fit to accuracy alone, whereas the Q-diffusion model also has to account for the response times and gives up a little accuracy fit to do so. The 2PL cannot predict response times at all. The model-implied mean response time can be checked per class. Plug-in scores compress person variance, so these predictions are rough: they are close for the 2D classes (within about 0.15 s) and about 0.3–0.4 s too slow for the 3D classes.

pred |> summarise(`observed mean RT (s)` = mean(rt_s), `predicted mean RT (s)` = mean(rt_q), .by = item_uid) |>
  arrange(item_uid) |> mutate(across(-item_uid, \(z) round(z, 2)))

6. Person parameters

persons |> summarise(across(c(gamma, theta, theta_irt, age), list(mean = mean, sd = sd), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "stat"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(mean|sd)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat) |> mutate(across(-variable, f3))

Relation to the paper’s ability score and to age

persons |> select(`Q: theta (speed of accumulation)` = theta, `Q: gamma (caution)` = gamma,
                  `2PL theta` = theta_irt, age) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise", method = "spearman") |> round(2)
##                                  Q: theta (speed of accumulation)
## Q: theta (speed of accumulation)                             1.00
## Q: gamma (caution)                                           0.35
## 2PL theta                                                    0.87
## age                                                          0.43
##                                  Q: gamma (caution) 2PL theta  age
## Q: theta (speed of accumulation)               0.35      0.87 0.43
## Q: gamma (caution)                             1.00      0.56 0.02
## 2PL theta                                      0.56      1.00 0.35
## age                                            0.02      0.35 1.00
long <- persons |>
  mutate(`Q-diffusion: log theta` = log(theta), `Q-diffusion: log gamma` = log(gamma), `2PL theta` = theta_irt) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Q-diffusion: log theta`, `Q-diffusion: log gamma`, `2PL theta`), names_to = "score") |>
  group_by(score) |> mutate(z = as.numeric(scale(value))) |> ungroup()
ggplot(long, aes(age, z, colour = score, fill = score)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, k = 5)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Standardised score", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)

ggplot(persons, aes(theta_irt, log(theta), colour = age)) + geom_point(alpha = .5, size = .8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() + labs(x = "2PL theta (paper)", y = "Q-diffusion log theta")

Drift rate \(\theta\) tracks the paper’s ability scores (Spearman .87) and increases with age (.43, against .35 for the 2PL score). The boundary parameter \(\gamma\) is unrelated to age (.02), so the age gain here comes from faster accumulation of evidence rather than from a shift in the speed-accuracy trade-off. \(\gamma\) also correlates positively with ability (.35 with \(\theta\), .56 with the 2PL score). Section 7 shows that \(\gamma\) is mostly an overall response-speed parameter: it correlates .89 with a run’s mean log RT. Read it as the level of the child’s response times (slow, careful responders have a high \(\gamma\)), not as a clean caution trait.

Differences between datasets

persons |> summarise(n = n(), age = mean(age), `2PL theta` = mean(theta_irt, na.rm = TRUE),
                      `log theta` = mean(log(theta)), `log gamma` = mean(log(gamma)), .by = dataset) |>
  mutate(across(-c(dataset, n), \(z) round(z, 2)))
# Dataset order of log theta matches the 2PL ordering (mpieva-de > western-ca > bogota > rural); log gamma differs little.
# How much of each score does age explain (spline in age)?
r2 <- \(y) summary(lm(y ~ splines::ns(age, 3), data = persons))$r.squared
c(`2PL theta` = r2(persons$theta_irt), `Q: log theta` = r2(log(persons$theta)), `Q: log gamma` = r2(log(persons$gamma))) |> round(3)
##    2PL theta Q: log theta Q: log gamma 
##        0.134        0.198        0.003

7. Do the paper’s age, sex and site results replicate with the diffusion scores?

05_diffirt_paper_analyses.R runs the paper’s ability model, score ~ age * sex * site + (1 | user_id) with sex sum-coded and average marginal effects over the observed runs, on five scores: the 2PL \(\theta\), the diffusion \(\log\theta\) and \(\log\gamma\), and, as descriptive anchors, each run’s accuracy and mean log RT. Effects are in SD units of each score. The model is fit on the 929 runs the paper uses for this analysis. The 2PL row reproduces the paper (age 0.33 per year in raw units = 0.23 SD; sex difference 0.00, \(p\) = .998).

pr <- read_rds(here("models/diffirt_paper_results.rds"))
pr$effects |>
  filter(effect %in% c("age (per year)", "sex (Male - Female)", "age slope: Male - Female")) |>
  transmute(measure, effect, est = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)%s", estimate_sd, se_sd, ifelse(p < .05, "*", ""))) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = effect, values_from = est)

(* = \(p < .05\), uncorrected for the five scores.)

  • Age. Drift \(\log\theta\) grows by 0.26 SD per year, close to the 2PL value of 0.23. The age \(\times\) sex interaction is null for every score. \(\log\gamma\) has only a small age trend (0.06 SD per year) and mean log RT none, so the age gain is carried by \(\theta\).
  • Sex. There is no sex difference in 2PL ability or in drift \(\theta\) (boys +0.07 SD, \(p\) = .18), and none in accuracy. Boys have lower \(\gamma\) (−0.13 SD, \(p\) = .036) and shorter mean log RT (−0.17 SD, \(p\) = .009). This matches the paper’s finding that boys are faster but not more accurate, and it puts the speed difference in the boundary/response-level parameter, not in ability. The \(\gamma\) result is nominal (\(p\) = .036 among five scores), and \(\gamma\) is highly correlated with mean log RT (Spearman .89 across runs), so it adds little beyond the RT result itself.
pr$effects |>
  filter(startsWith(effect, "sex within") | effect == "sex (Male - Female)",
         measure %in% c("2PL theta", "Diffusion log theta (drift)", "Diffusion log gamma (boundary)", "Mean log RT")) |>
  mutate(where = ifelse(effect == "sex (Male - Female)", "All sites", sub("sex within ", "", effect)),
         where = factor(where, levels = rev(c("All sites", "mpieva-de", "uniandes-co-bogota", "uniandes-co-rural", "western-ca"))),
         measure = factor(measure, levels = c("2PL theta", "Diffusion log theta (drift)", "Diffusion log gamma (boundary)", "Mean log RT"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate_sd, where, colour = where == "All sites")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = estimate_sd - 1.96 * se_sd, xmax = estimate_sd + 1.96 * se_sd)) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "grey45"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Male - Female (SD units, 95% CI)", y = NULL)

Sex differences by site are small and imprecise for every score. Drift shows a nominally positive male difference in Bogotá (+0.21 SD, SE 0.10) that the 2PL does not (+0.10, SE 0.11). With 16 site-by-score estimates this is not distinguishable from noise.

sites <- pr$effects |> filter(startsWith(effect, "site:")) |>
  filter(measure %in% c("2PL theta", "Diffusion log theta (drift)", "Diffusion log gamma (boundary)", "Mean log RT")) |>
  mutate(contrast = sub("site: ", "", effect))
sites |> select(measure, contrast, estimate_sd) |> pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = estimate_sd) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(z) round(z, 2)))
ggplot(sites |> filter(measure != "2PL theta") |>
         left_join(sites |> filter(measure == "2PL theta") |> select(contrast, theta_2pl = estimate_sd), by = "contrast"),
       aes(theta_2pl, estimate_sd, colour = contrast)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey70") + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18)) +
  labs(x = "Site contrast in 2PL theta (SD)", y = "Site contrast in diffusion score or RT (SD)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

  • Sites. The drift contrasts are almost identical to the 2PL contrasts (for example Bogotá − Leipzig −0.79 vs −0.82 SD; rural − Leipzig −1.10 vs −1.20 SD), so the site ordering is unchanged. \(\log\gamma\) and mean log RT instead separate Leipzig (mpieva-de, remote home testing) from the other three sites, which fits the paper’s account of slower baseline RTs there. The model therefore puts the site difference in RT level into \(\gamma\), not into drift, so \(\theta\) is not inflated or deflated by the slow-RT site. The paper does not interpret site differences in ability, and this does not change that.
  • Repeated runs. The random-intercept model reaches a conditional \(R^2\) of 0.822 for the 2PL and 0.694 for drift \(\theta\) (marginal 0.357 vs 0.382). The difference is the user-level share, which comes from a small group of children with more than one run. Treat it as a hint that drift is less stable across runs, not as a result.

8. Summary and caveats

  • The recipe is: build person-by-item matrices, constrain parameters within item classes, start \(T_{er}\) at about 0.3 s, and run diffIRT(model = "Q") with a couple of quadrature settings. The optimised build fits all 1,158 assessments in about 10 s.
  • The difficulty-like parameter \(v_i\) orders the item classes like the 2PL difficulty (\(r = .96\); \(.89\) within the 2D classes). The 2PL discrimination does not carry over to a Q-diffusion parameter, because difficulty and slope are not separate parameters in the Q model, and the two disagree in direction (section 5).
  • The Q-diffusion person drift \(\theta\) is highly correlated with the 2PL ability and a bit more strongly related to age (\(R^2\) .20 vs .13 with a spline in age). The 2PL predicts accuracy slightly better, and the Q model also predicts the class mean RTs reasonably well.
  • The paper’s age, sex and site results carry over to the diffusion drift score (section 7): same age trend, no sex or age \(\times\) sex effect on ability, and the same site ordering. The boys-are-faster result shows up in \(\gamma\), which is mostly a response-time level parameter (r = .89 with mean log RT) and is not a separate caution trait.
  • Caveats: standard errors are probably optimistic; 3D non-decision time is weakly identified (the 3D RTs are long); the section-5 comparison is across 12 classes; person scores are EAP estimates and the fit checks are in-sample; and equality of estimates between the optimised and the original diffIRT could not be checked because the original never finished.
